newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SCA profit highlights forest industry woes.
newsitem.headline: SCA profit highlights forest industry woes.

text.p: Sweden's largest forestry company, Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget (SCA), underlined on Thursday the industry's problems with costs and uncertain prices by posting a sharp drop in 1996 profits.
SCA reported a profit after financial items of 3.57 billion crowns ($492 million), a 38 percent fall from 1995.

Echoing the gloomy tone of rival Stora which also reported a heavy profit fall, SCA said major uncertainty for pulp and paper price developments remained for 1997 although it planned to raise fine paper prices on February 1.
"The recovery is taking place from a low level at a slow pace. Major uncertainty remains for price developments surrounding pulp and recycling paper," SCA said in a statement.
Analysts said the industry needed to focus on cutting costs as the prospect of price rises remained distant.
SCA's report contained little good news for the industry, which is expected to see profits squeezed throughout 1997.
"1997 will still be a weak year, much like 1996. But this year will be stronger in the second half and 1998 should be better," one Stockholm-based analyst said.

Based on turnover of 55.41 billion crowns against 65.32 billion a year earlier, SCA is Sweden's largest forestry group. Market consensus had put its profit after financial items at 3.52 billion crowns.
SCA shares edged down one crown to 143 crowns after the result was announced but were flat in later trade.
In the Swedish forestry sector, MoDo is due to report its 1996 results on February 19 and AssiDoman AB on February 20.
Analysts said SCA was somewhat better off than other companies because its hygiene products division cushioned it from falls in pulp prices.
Profit for hygiene products, the company's largest unit that includes fluff and clinical products as well as tissue, rose to 2.32 billion crowns in 1996 from 1.37 billion in 1995.
This was a larger increase than expected, analysts said.

"Relative to Stora it's in a much more favourable position because SCA is fibre-short. Tissue is not a product that is too sensitive to decreased pulp prices," said Denis Christie, forestry analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
Stora, Sweden's second largest forestry company, posted on Wednesday a lower than expected 1996 profit after financial items of 2.35 billion crowns against 8.02 billion in 1995.
"The companies that will do best are those that are getttng to grip with the cost structure and getting costs under control. I think SCA is doing this," Christie said.
SCA said it was working on this is in its fine papers division, which posted an operating loss of 480 million crowns after an operating profit of 1.30 billion a year earlier.
"Although it was a loss, it was a smaller loss than I expected," one analyst said.

"An extensive efficiency enhancement and improvement programme was initiated within SCA Fine Paper which, within a three-year period and with marginal investments, is expected to improve earnings by about 500 million crowns," SCA said. ($1=7.26 crowns)
